India opt to bowl despite batting-friendly pitch

Naman Dhir makes his ODI debut for India after captain Shubman Gill won the toss and elected to bowl first against West Indies in the opening ODI of the series at the Greenfield International Stadium in Thiruvananthapuram on Sunday.Dhir has been handed his maiden ODI cap as India look to begin the three-match series with a win. The Indian team has also included Gurnoor Brar, while Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Ruturaj Gaikwad and KL Rahul feature in the playing XI.Gill explained that India preferred to chase on what appeared to be a decent batting surface."We're gonna bowl first, looks like a decent surface. Will come better under the lights, so want to chase. We have got a decent combination, four bowlers and two allrounders. 20-odd matches to go for the World Cup, so good for us to test the combination," Gill said after winning the toss.West Indies captain Shai Hope also said his side would have preferred to bowl first, expecting the surface to improve under lights."We are gonna bowl first, looks like a decent surface. Will come better under the lights, so want to chase," Hope said.Rohit Sharma, Shubman Gill (c), Virat Kohli, Ruturaj Gaikwad, KL Rahul (w), Naman Dhir, Ravindra Jadeja, Nitish Kumar Reddy, Gurnoor Brar, Kuldeep Yadav, Prasidh KrishnaJohn Campbell, Justin Greaves, Keacy Carty, Shai Hope (w/c), Amir Jangoo, Jewel Andrew, Roston Chase, Matthew Forde, Gudakesh Motie, Alzarri Joseph, Jayden SealesThe pitch report suggested that conditions could favour the batters at the Greenfield International Stadium. The surface is made from black Mandya clay from neighbouring Karnataka and has a hard base with minimal grass covering. According to the pitch report, the hard surface should allow the ball to come onto the bat nicely, while the limited grass is expected to reduce lateral movement for the seamers.The square boundaries measure around 65 metres on either side, while the straight boundary is approximately 74 metres.The pitch is also expected to offer extra bounce because of the nature of the black clay. With little grass on the surface, the ball is expected to travel through to the bat rather than losing energy after pitching.
Article Summary: Naman Dhir makes his ODI debut for India after captain Shubman Gill won the toss and elected to bowl first against West Indies. Dhir has been handed his maiden ODI cap as India look to begin the three-match series with a win. The pitch report suggested that conditions could favour the batters at the Greenfield International Stadium.

Article Title: Asian Games 2026: India’s 44-year wait ends as Sawan Barwal wins silver in men’s marathon
Article Text:
India's Sawan Barwal reacts after his second place finish in the men's marathon at the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Lee Jin-man)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Historic medal for Indian athletics

Sawan Barwal scripted history at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya on Saturday, winning silver in the men’s marathon and ending India’s 44-year wait for a medal in the event. He clocked a personal best of 2:11:37, finishing 48 seconds behind Japan’s Ichitaka Yamashita, who won gold in 2:10:49. China’s Peiyou Feng took bronze with 2:12:13.The marathon started at 4 a.m. IST with 19 runners, including Barwal and fellow Indian Kartik Karkera. Barwal quickly established himself among the leaders and was in second place at the halfway mark with a timing of 1:05:54. He continued to hold his position as the race entered its final stages, reaching the 35-kilometre mark in second.With around seven kilometres left, Barwal was still chasing Yamashita. The Japanese runner eventually opened up a gap, but Barwal maintained his pace and stayed firmly in silver-medal position. He finished with a timing of 2:11:37, securing India’s first Asian Games marathon medal since the 1982 Delhi Games and the country’s first medal in the event on foreign soil.The silver adds to Barwal’s growing record. In April, he broke Shivnath Singh’s 48-year-old national marathon record at the NN Marathon Rotterdam.His latest performance now converts that record-setting form into a major international medal.Barwal’s silver is India’s fourth Asian Games marathon medal. Chhota Singh won gold and Surat Singh Mathur took bronze at the inaugural 1951 Games, while Hosur Kukkappa Seetharan won another bronze in 1982.The other Indian runner, Kartik Karkera, finished 17th among 19 competitors with a time of 2:22:41.
Article Summary: Sawan Barwal won silver in the men's marathon at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya. He clocked a personal best of 2:11:37, finishing 48 seconds behind Japan’s Ichitaka Yamashita, who won gold in 2:10:49. It is India's first Asian Games marathon medal since the 1982 Delhi Games.

Article Title: 'Not too much pressure': How Zhu Jiner turned struggles in India into taking China closer to Chess Olympiad gold | Exclusive
Article Text:
China's Zhu Jiner at Chess Olympiad (Photo by Michal Walusza for FIDE)

Finding warmth amid a difficult campaign

From four-year-old beginner to China’s Board 1

Steering the ship in Samarkand

ALSO READ:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

(Indian women's team takes on China in the penultimate round of Chess Olympiad on Saturday.)

NEW DELHI: The 46th edition of the Chess Olympiad is currently edging towards its climax in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. In the women's section, one team has pulled clear of the rest, and it is China, the comfortable leaders at the moment. And if anything doesn't go south, it will be the Chinese girls donning the gold medals around their necks at the end of 11 rounds of play. But do you know the most interesting thing in it? China don't even have their strongest players in the event.As per the current FIDE ratings, none of the world top three, which include Hou Yifan, the current women's world champion Ju Wenjun, and Lei Tingjie, is part of this Chinese side. Zhu Jiner, the world no. 4, is thus on Board 1, facing the toughest of the top board opponents at this Samarkand Olympiad. And she has risen to the challenge, remaining unbeaten throughout, a complete turnaround from her form at the Global Chess League (GCL) in India just a couple of weeks earlier.Just before the Olympiad, Jiner was part of the two-time GCL champion Triveni Continental Kings, who had a torrid event as they finished second from bottom in the group stage this time.Jiner's performance was not up to the mark either, with the 23-year-old Grandmaster winning just one, losing four and drawing five games in the tournament.The on-board results, coupled with the hectic schedule, meant little time or urge for her to enjoy the city of Bengaluru, the host of this fourth edition of GCL.Despite her struggles on the board, Jiner maintained a deep appreciation for the host nation. "This is my first time in Bengaluru, and overall, I’ve had a very good impression of the city. The weather is also very pleasant," Jiner told TimesofIndia.com during an exclusive interaction."Since I’m here mainly to compete in the Global Chess League, there’s been quite a lot of time spent on matches and preparation, so I haven’t really had much time to go out. When I have a game, most of my energy is focused on the competition."Bengaluru was simply the latest stop in Jiner’s long-standing relationship with Indian chess venues, having previously played across the country's major hubs."I’ve been to India several times before. I’ve visited New Delhi, Pune, Mumbai, and now Bengaluru, all for international chess tournaments," she recounted. "What I like most about India is how passionate people are about chess. Whether they’re players or fans, you can really feel their love for the game. For example, during this Global Chess League, the players have received such a warm welcome from the local fans. Every day, when we come out of the playing venue, there are so many chess fans waiting to get autographs or take photos with their idols. That atmosphere has left a very deep impression on me."Jiner also noted the broader cultural and competitive ties between the two Asian superpowers, acknowledging the explosive growth of Indian chess talent on the global stage."I think India has a very long and rich history and culture. I’ve heard some Indian mythological stories as well," she observed. "At the same time, India is a very vibrant and rapidly developing country, and there is a lot of trade and exchange between the two countries (India and China). As far as modern chess is concerned, India has developed incredibly quickly over the past few years, especially when it comes to the younger generation. There are now many very talented young Indian players, and they have achieved excellent results in international competitions again and again."Jiner's journey to leading China's national team on Board 1 in Samarkand was built on decades of steady progression. "I was introduced to chess when I was about four years old. At first, it was very simple, I just thought the game was interesting and enjoyed playing it," Jiner recalled."Then, when I was around seven, I joined the Zhejiang team and began receiving more systematic training. Later, I joined the national team and gradually started competing at higher and higher levels. Actually, there wasn’t one particular moment when I suddenly decided, 'I want to become a professional chess player.' It happened gradually. Over time, chess became a very important part of my life, and eventually becoming a professional player felt like a natural choice for me. "Her personal trajectory mirrors the unique structure of Chinese chess. "Chess came to China relatively late. It has been around for many years now, but compared with some other sports, it is still a relatively niche sport," Jiner explained."I’m not very familiar with the current development system for young Chinese players, but I think for a little girl who is just starting to learn chess, the most important thing is to first develop a genuine love for the game. The professional path is actually very long, and there will be many difficulties along the way. If you really love the sport, that’s what will help you keep going."That resilience proved essential as China arrived in Samarkand without its standard contingent of World Champions. Leading an understrength team, Jiner reframed the narrative, turning the absence of superstars into a source of resolve."I think China has some of the strongest female players in the world, and overall, the team has consistently been among the strongest," Jiner noted before the start of the tournament. "However, this time, the Chinese team hasn’t been able to compete at the Olympiad with its most complete and strongest lineup, which I personally feel is a little unfortunate."Rather than letting the pressure of top-board responsibility overwhelm her squad after the setback in India, Jiner embraced the lowered expectations, which has worked well for her and her team so far."Of course, even under these circumstances, the Chinese women's team is still a very strong team. But there are many strong teams at this Olympiad, and I think the competition between them will be extremely intense. So I wouldn’t consider China the biggest favourite to win the title.For us, that actually means there isn’t too much pressure. We’ll prepare carefully for each round, focus on the opponent in front of us, try to play at our best, and aim for a good result. "Jiner may not have considered China the biggest favourite to win the title. But that pragmatic, round-by-round focus is now on the verge of delivering one of the most remarkable gold medal runs in modern Olympiad history.
Article Summary: World no. 4 Zhu Jiner is leading China's women's team at the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. The 23-year-old Grandmaster is unbeaten on Board 1, a complete turnaround from her form at the Global Chess League (GCL) in India just a couple of weeks earlier.

Article Title: Week after losing coach, grieving Diya Chitale gets a moment to savour at Asian Games
Article Text:
Manush Shah and Diya Chitale (File photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: For Diya Chitale, the last seven days have been an emotional roller coaster. Exactly a week after losing Peter Engel, her coach since 2015, Diya stood on the Asian Games podium in Nagoya with the bronze medal around her neck, alongside Manush Shah. The duo had their moments against China’s top pairing of Wang Chuqin and Sun Yingsha before going down (0-4) 8-11, 5-11, 8-11, 2-11 in the mixed doubles semifinals at Sky Hall Toyota in Nagoya, settling for bronze. Despite the loss, Diya and Shah secured India’s first table-tennis medal of the ongoing Games.For Diya, Engel — who died on Sept 18 at 72 — was far more than a coach. “I had been working with Engel sir since 2015 and he is the person who completely developed my game. He was my go-to person for everything in TT,” she told TOI from Nagoya. Apart from the personal tragedy, there was also a lean spell for Diya and Shah to overcome. The world No. 8 mixed doubles pair had won two titles and finished runners-up once early in 2026, but their results dipped from June onwards. “I always believed that we are among the top few pairs and we can beat any pair on our day,” she said. Their belief was tested earlier on Friday.Drawn against Hong Kong’s world No. 4 Doo Hoi Kem and Wong Chun Ting, a pair they had lost to three times, the Indians knew execution had to be precise. They delivered, winning 3-1 (11-6, 13-15, 11-9, 11-5) to assure the nation its first TT medal of the Games before losing in semifinals. “We had played against them thrice and lost all our matches, but the last two matches were pretty close,” Diya said. “Hence we knew that if we had a clear strategy and if we could execute that well, we had a good chance.And we were able to do that today.”The medal carries weight far beyond the colour. It is India’s second Asian Games mixed doubles medal, after Sharath Kamal and Manika Batra’s bronze in Jakarta in 2018. “Winning a medal at the Games in our sport is huge and extra sweet since all the powerhouses in TT come from Asia — China, Japan, South Korea and so on,” she said. Diya dedicated her medal to Engel, paying her a personal tribute. “It would have been wonderful for him to see me achieve this today. This medal is for him.”
Article Summary: Diya Chitale and Manush Shah secure India's first table-tennis medal of the Games. They beat Hong Kong's world No. 4 Doo Hoi Kem and Wong Chun Ting 3-1. But they lost in semifinals to China's top pairing of Wang Chuqin and Sun Yingsha.

Article Title: D Gukesh ‘tricks’ Germany, keeps Indian challenge alive at Chess Olympiad
Article Text:
D Gukesh (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Gukesh spooked Alexander Donchenko, helping India score a seemingly unlikely victory over overnight joint leaders Germany in the ninth round of the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand on Friday.The win helped India move to 15 match-points, one behind leaders and hosts Uzbekistan (16), who humbled USA. Nodirbek Yakubboev scored another crucial win for the hosts, this time over Hans Niemann. Uzbekistan’s second-strength team and Armenia are also level with India on points with just two rounds remaining.India women (15 points) humbled Uzbekistan 3-1 but are still trailing China (17) by two match-points. China, who have not fielded their full-strength team, continued their march towards the gold medal with a win over Armenia, in which Zhu Jiner and Lu Miaoyi scored full points.The draw between Kazakhstan and Mongolia (15 each) also helped India, as neither could overtake them. Divya Deshmukh and Vanitka Agrawal, individual gold medallists in the last Olympiad, scripted the success of the Indian women as they defeated lower-rated opponents.B Savitha Shri’s stunning sequence of seven successive wins came to an end with a draw against Guildona Karimova (Elo 2242), while K Humpy held her own on the top board.World champion Gukesh once again showed why he is such a dangerous rival. Germany, somewhat surprisingly, decided to rest Rasmus Svane, who had two successive wins in the preceding rounds, and chose to field Donchenko against Gukesh.The 28-year-old German almost justified the faith shown in him by pushing Gukesh to a corner. However, he then gave too much importance to Gukesh’s h-pawn and misplaced his pieces.ALSO READ: 'Not too much pressure': How Zhu Jiner turned struggles in India into taking China closer to Chess Olympiad gold | Exclusive While this drama was unfolding, Nihal Sarin had already drawn his game against Frederik Svane despite flirting with danger and mental abyss. R Praggnanandhaa and Erigaisi Arjun were unable to break through the defences of Vincent Keymer and Matthias Blubaum respectively.Arjun had even sacrificed his knight but reached a queen-and-extra-pawns versus queen, bishop-and-pawns endgame. However, with Gukesh turning the tables, the draws by Arjun and Praggnanandhaa were no longer a losing cause.
Article Summary: Gukesh spooked Alexander Donchenko, helping India score a seemingly unlikely victory over overnight joint leaders Germany. The win helped India move to 15 match-points, one behind leaders and hosts Uzbekistan (16), who humbled USA. Uzbekistan’s second-strength team and Armenia are also level with India on points with just two rounds remaining.

Article Title: Asian Games 2026: Joshna Chinappa, Velavan Senthilkumar settle for bronze in Squash mixed doubles
Article Text:
India's Joshana Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar settle for bronze. (PTI Photo)

India lose first game by narrowest margin

Joshna, Velavan hit back in style

India’s Joshna Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar came agonisingly close to a place in the Asian Games mixed doubles final, losing a dramatic semifinal to Hong Kong’s Tang Ming Hong and Lee Ka Yi 1-2 (10-11, 11-2, 11-10).The Indian pair looked to have one foot in the final after fighting back from a tight opening-game defeat and dominating the second. They then led 9-7 in the decider and had three match points, only for the Hong Kong pair to stage a stunning comeback and snatch the contest in a nerve-wracking finish.The defeat meant Joshna and Velavan had to settle for a bronze medal.The opening game was a tense battle with neither pair able to establish a significant advantage. Joshna and Velavan edged ahead at one stage, but Tang and Lee responded with three straight points to move 9-8 ahead. The Indians quickly levelled at 9-9 before Hong Kong earned game point.India fought back again to make it 10-10, but Tang and Lee won the next point to take the game 11-10 and move within one game of the final.The Indians responded emphatically in the second game. Joshna and Velavan came out aggressively, looking to finish points quickly rather than getting drawn into the long rallies that had characterised the opening game.They raced into a 3-0 lead and extended it to 7-2. From there, they did not give Hong Kong another point, closing out the game 11-2 to force a decider. Three match points slip away in dramatic deciderThe deciding game produced the most intense action of the contest. Joshna and Velavan initially trailed 2-5 but fought back to make it 4-5. The game then turned into a battle of attrition, with long rallies and several 'lets', where a point is replayed because of an obstruction, adding to the tension.The Indians eventually levelled at 6-6 before taking control. They moved 8-7 ahead and then stretched their lead to 9-7, with Velavan producing some outstanding defensive work. At 9-7, India had three match points but could not convert them. Tang and Lee held their nerve to win the next three points and level the game at 10-10.The next rally was fiercely contested and ended in controversy. India initially appeared to have won the point, with Velavan briefly celebrating, but the point was disallowed. Hong Kong then won the following point to complete a remarkable 11-10 comeback and book their place in the final.

Article Title: Khalid Jamil's India hold Panama to memorable 1-1 draw
Article Text:
India's Ryan Williams, right, shoots at goal as Panama's Roderick Miller defends during an international friendly soccer match between India and Panama in Bengaluru, India, Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

It was an unforgettable Friday for the Indian football fans as the Blue Tigers fought on level terms with World Cup participants Panama, forcing a 1-1 draw from their famous visitors at Sree Kanteerava Stadium here.Panama, who played against Ghana, Croatia and England at the World Cup, had to dig deep as they rallied to avoid defeat against 138-ranked India in the FIFA international friendly.The hosts took the lead against the run of play, against a team 94 places above them in the world rankings, thanks to a clinical finish by striker Ryan Williams in the 41st minute. The visitors, who started with just three World Cuppers, made changes at the start of second half and the complexion of the game soon changed.Panama found the equaliser in the 67th minute after the entry of Azarias Londono, Jiovani Ramos and Omar Valencia in the second half. Valencia, the defender who plays for the New York Red Bulls in Major League Soccer, fired Panama’s equaliser with a long-range stunner.It was a well worked goal as Londono relayed the ball to defender Eduardo Gomez who found Valencia with a clear view of the goal. India wasted a golden chance in the 79th minute but Edmund Lalrindika failed to apply finishing touches to a perfectly-weighted pass from Ashique Kuruniyan.Sedate first half: Panama coach Thomas Christiansen was enjoying the cool Bengaluru weather, following a brief spell of rain which took the temperature to 22 degrees Celsius, watching his team press against a dogged Indian defence before his team went behind. The smile on his face vanished as he walked to the dressing room when the referee blew the half-time whistle as Williams put India ahead four minutes before the break.Until then, the visitors held the upper hand with more possession (58 per cent) and more shots (6), two of which were on target. However, the Indian team ensured they gave their famous rivals a good fight. It was a superb result for India coach Khalid Jamil who will now look forward to the same spirited show against former world champions Uruguay and Brazil.
Article Summary: India drew 1-1 with Panama at Sree Kanteerava Stadium in Bengaluru. Ryan Williams opened the scoring for the hosts in the 41st minute. Omar Valencia equalised in the 67th minute with a long-range stunner.

Article Title: Shock exit for Satwik-Chirag as Asian Games title defence ends in first round
Article Text:
Asian Games 2026: Thailand's Sukphun-Pakkapon stun defending champions Satwik-Chirag in R32

Tanisha-Dhruv advance

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Defending champions Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty suffered a major setback at the Asian Games, crashing out in the first round after losing to Thailand’s Pakkapon Teeraratsakul and Peeratchai Sukphun on Friday.The Indian pair started strongly, winning the opening game 21-12, but failed to maintain their momentum. The world No. 36 Thai duo fought back to win the next two games 21-19, 21-14 in 64 minutes.Satwik and Chirag looked set for a routine victory after dominating the first game, but the Thais made the most of the Indians’ errors in the second. With the score at 18-19, Satwik’s return went into the net to give Thailand a game point. The Indians saved one, but Pakkapon produced a superb cross-court winner to level the match.The deciding game turned one-sided as Satwik and Chirag appeared increasingly fatigued. Their returns lacked their usual power, forcing the world’s best attacking pair into an unfamiliar defensive role as the Thais repeatedly unleashed smashes.The defeat came after a demanding schedule and limited recovery time. Satwik said the team had returned late from the previous night’s event.“Quite patchy... We know these situations will happen. It will get tense because it will be tricky playing continuously in the team event. We were here till 12 last night,” Satwik told reporters.He also admitted that the pair needed to improve their mental approach.“It’s the mental part. Whenever we are mentally free, I think no one can beat us. But when we are stuck anywhere, we give opponents a chance to beat us,” he said.There was better news for India in mixed doubles, with Tanisha Crasto and Dhruv Kapila reaching the quarterfinals after two contrasting wins.They began with a comfortable 21-8, 21-7 victory over Maldives’ Nibal Ahmed and Aminath Nabeeha Abdul Razzaq in just 21 minutes. They were then pushed hard by Malaysia’s Shevon Jemie Lai and Soon Huat Goh but held their nerve to win 22-20, 24-22 in an hour.Tanisha and Dhruv will face China’s Yan Zhe Feng and Dongping Huang in the quarterfinals.World Championships bronze medallists Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand and Unnati Hooda also won their opening-round matches. Hooda defeated North Korea’s Mi Song Yu 21-9, 21-10 in 30 minutes.India’s second men’s doubles pair, Hariharan Amsakarunan and MR Arjun, however, lost 14-21, 11-21 to second-seeded Indonesians Fajar Alfian and Muhammad Shohi
Article Summary: Defending champions Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty lose to Thailand's Pakkapon Teeraratsakul and Peeratchai Sukphun. World No. 36 Thai duo fought back to win the next two games 21-19, 21-14 in 64 minutes. Tanisha Crasto and Dhruv Kapila reach the quarterfinals after two contrasting wins.

Article Title: DDCA joint secretary raises concerns over Delhi selector, support staff appointments
Article Text:
A view of the Arun Jaitley Stadium in New Delhi. (PTI Photo/Kamal Kishore)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Delhi & District Cricket Association (DDCA) joint secretary Amit Grover has formally raised reservations over the proposed appointments of Varun Sood and Manu Nayyar as part of the Delhi cricket setup, questioning whether they meet the prescribed eligibility criteria.In an email sent to members of the Cricket Advisory Committee (CAC) on Friday, a copy of which TimesofIndia.com has, Grover said he wanted to place his concerns on record before the selection process concluded. He urged the committee to examine the relevant records and applicable rules before making any final decision on the proposed appointments. The email is addressed to members of the CAC and copied to the DDCA top brass.“With regard to the proposed appointments of coaches and selectors, I wish to formally place on record my reservations concerning the proposed appointment of Mr. Varun Sood and Mr. Manu Nayyar, particularly with regard to their eligibility and compliance with the prescribed criteria,” Grover wrote in the email.Manu Nayyar has been appointed as selector for the senior men’s team and Varun Sood as assistant coach for the men’s U-19 team.It is worth noting that there was an issue with Nayyar's availability last season as he was reportedly missing due to committments in an overseas league, when the teams were being picked at DDCA.“All the rules have been followed diligently. Everyone who has been appointed has played cricket at the highest level. They have been in the system for a long time. Manu Nayyar is yet to complete his five-year term, whereas Varun has recently retired from playing cricket and knows a thing or two about how modern-day cricket functions. We are all thinking about the betterment of Delhi cricket, and these accusations are needless,” said a recipient of the email.TimesofIndia.com reached out to DDCA secretary Ashok Sharma for a comment but received no response.Former India wicketkeeper Vijay Dahiya has been reappointed as head coach of the Delhi Ranji Trophy team as the DDCA named coaches, mentors and High Performance Centre staff, with several former players and their sons also finding assignments in the appointments. There are 22 coaches, including head coaches, assistant coaches, bowling coaches and fielding coaches, appointed across the senior men’s team to the U-14 level, while 18 have been appointed across various women’s teams.Meanwhile, Grover emphasised that the concerns had been communicated before the completion of the selection process and, therefore, should be considered by the CAC before any appointment was finalised. He said the committee should satisfy itself that all eligibility conditions and prescribed criteria had been complied with.The DDCA joint secretary also questioned the proposed composition of the selection panel, pointing out that it appeared to substantially comprise the same selectors who were associated with the process last year.His concern comes against the backdrop of what he described as disappointing performances by Delhi cricket. Grover acknowledged that continuity could have its merits but urged the CAC to exercise “greater care and circumspection” while selecting coaches and selectors. He said recent performances, along with eligibility, experience and the overall requirements of Delhi cricket, should be taken into account when making the appointments.“I therefore request the CAC to independently examine all relevant records and applicable criteria before taking any final decision,” Grover wrote, while also requesting that his communication be treated as part of the official record of the selection and appointment process.
Article Summary: Delhi & District Cricket Association (DDCA) joint secretary Amit Grover has formally raised reservations over the proposed appointments of Varun Sood and Manu Nayyar. Grover questioned whether they meet the prescribed eligibility criteria. He urged the committee to examine the relevant records and applicable rules before making any final decision.

Article Title: Asian Games 2026: Niraj Kumar, Rudrankksh Patil, Aishwary Pratap Singh win silver in 50m rifle 3 positions team event
Article Text:
Aishwary Pratap Singh, Niraj Kumar and Rudrankksh Patil (Image credit: Agencies)

NEW DELHI: India's Niraj Kumar, Rudrankksh Patil and Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar won the silver medal in the men's 50m rifle 3 positions team event at the Asian Games 2026.The Indian trio finished with a total score of 1762-94x to finish second behind China.India scored 294 in the first kneeling series and 587 after the second kneeling series. They then added 297 points in the first prone series to reach 884, before moving to 1180 after the second prone series.In the standing position, India scored 291 in the first series and 291 in the second to finish with a total of 1762 points.China won the gold medal with 1766-95x, finishing four points ahead of India.South Korea took the bronze medal with a total score of 1751-87x.
Article Summary: India's Niraj Kumar, Rudrankksh Patil and Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar won the silver medal in the men's 50m rifle 3 positions team event at the Asian Games 2026. The Indian trio finished with a total score of 1762-94x to finish second behind China.

Article Title: Asian Games: Aishwary Pratap Singh finishes fifth, Niraj Kumar eighth as India miss 50m rifle 3P individual medal after team silver
Article Text:
Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar (ANI Photo)

Aishwary and Niraj fail to convert qualification form into medals

India’s shooting tally reaches 10 medals

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India’s shooters missed out on a medal in the men’s 50m rifle 3 positions individual event at the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya on Friday, despite securing silver in the team competition earlier in the day. Asian record holder Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar finished fifth in the individual final, while Niraj Kumar came last among the eight finalists, bringing a disappointing end to India’s campaign in the event.Aishwary, who had qualified third for the final, managed 327.6 points to finish fifth. Niraj, who had entered the final in fourth place in qualification, could only score 299 points to finish eighth.China’s Liu Yukun claimed gold with 360.5 points, setting a new Asian Games record. His compatriot Zhang Changhong took silver with 360.2 points, while Kazakhstan’s Islam Satpayev secured bronze with 348.3 points.The result was a setback for India after both shooters had shown promise in the qualification round. Aishwary, the Asian record holder, had finished third, while Niraj secured the fourth qualifying spot. However, neither could maintain that position in the final as China swept the top two places.The individual event disappointment followed India’s silver-medal finish in the men’s 50m rifle 3 positions team competition. Aishwary, Niraj and Rudrankksh Patil combined for a score of 1762-94x, finishing just behind China, who secured gold with 1766-95x. South Korea took bronze with 1751-87x.Aishwary scored 589-34x to finish third in the team qualification standings, while Niraj recorded 588-34x to place fourth. Rudrankksh, with 585-26x, finished ninth and missed out on a place in the individual final.India had won gold in the team event at the 2022 Asian Games but surrendered their title to China in Aichi-Nagoya.India’s shooting contingent has now collected 10 medals at the 2026 Asian Games, including one gold, five silver and four bronze medals. The only shooting gold so far came on Friday, when Suruchi and Kamaljeet won the 10m mixed air pistol event.The Indian pair defeated South Korea 484.6 to 478.0 in the final, with Iran taking bronze on 415.8 points. India’s winning score also broke the Asian record of 481.3, previously set by Uzbekistan at the Asian Shooting Championships in New Delhi earlier this year.India’s overall medal tally at the Games stood at 19 on Friday, comprising two gold, eight silver and nine bronze medals. The women’s cricket team had earlier secured India’s other gold, defeating Sri Lanka by 147 runs in the final.The rifle team silver added to India’s medal haul, but the failure to convert two strong qualification performances into an individual podium finish left the shooters without another medal in the event.
Article Summary: India's shooting contingent has now collected 10 medals at the 2026 Asian Games. Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar finished fifth in the individual final, while Niraj Kumar came last among the eight finalists. India’s overall medal tally at the Games stood at 19, comprising two gold, eight silver and nine bronze medals.

Article Title: 'I was distraught': Virat Kohli reveals defeat that was 'too tough to swallow'
Article Text:
Virat Kohli

'2019 was a jolt for us'

Kohli remembers 2023 dressing-room atmosphere

'I feel the same about the World Cup final'

Kohli's unfinished World Cup business

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India's recent ICC success may have brought an end to their long-standing trophy drought, but some World Cup defeats continue to remain difficult memories for Virat Kohli India won back-to-back T20 World Cup titles before adding the Champions Trophy, but the heartbreak of November 19, 2023 still remains fresh in the minds of ardent cricket followers. Rohit Sharma has spoken about that defeat on several occasions.For Kohli , though, the 2019 World Cup semifinal loss to New Zealand remains an even more painful experience.The semifinal in Manchester stretched across two days after persistent rain interrupted New Zealand's innings in the 47th over. The Black Caps returned the following day to finish on 239/8 before India fell 18 runs short in the chase.The match is particularly remembered for MS Dhoni's heartbreaking run-out by Martin Guptill in the 49th over.Bhuvneshwar Kumar, who took three wickets in the game, recently described the defeat as "heartbreaking". Kohli agreed with his former India team-mate, admitting that the loss left him distraught.“Playing Australia in the 2015 semifinal, you are very well aware of your strength and weaknesses and Australia is always difficult. We always knew that if it gets to a massive score, it will be tough, and that is what happened.They were phenomenal.“But 2019 was a jolt for us. 240... it rained out. Had we played that day, things would have been different. But next morning, fresh new ball attack. They got the best of the conditions and they put us under attack and they banked on the hesitation that we had.“That was too tough to swallow and process. I was distraught. After that I was totally gone mentally for a couple of months,” he told JioStar ahead of India’s first ODI against West Indies.Kohli viewed India's run to the 2023 World Cup final differently, describing the campaign as a "massive step forward" in terms of both talent and performance.More than the results, however, he remembered the atmosphere within the squad and the way the players responded to setbacks.“That whole World Cup was great, the environment was phenomenal. Within the team, you could see the camaraderie; everyone was happy playing for each other.“Even losing someone like Hardik early on, we never spoke about what would happen next although it was a big loss in terms of what he brings. But, Shami came and you know what he can do.“So, everyone had a feeling that it was our World Cup,” he added.India's campaign ultimately ended with a defeat to Australia in the final in Ahmedabad, another result that Kohli found difficult to process.He compared the feeling to the flashbacks he experienced after the 2016 IPL final, which continued until Royal Challengers Bengaluru won the IPL in 2025.“Before we won the IPL in 2025, I used to get flashbacks of the 2016 final. I feel the same about the World Cup final as well.“I was playing on 54 and had set myself up for a big hundred; like, if I got 140-150, we would be in a great position to win that game.“But as soon as I played on, it was very tough to process for many days. And you keep thinking about it.”Despite the painful memories, Kohli does not believe his World Cup journey is complete.“The thought will never cross my mind that the business I had is finished. As long as you’re playing, there is always something to look forward to. And I’m looking forward to the World Cup, looking at what lies ahead for me.“When the World Cup is played, when we play an ICC tournament, it has its own unique challenge, because you face different opponents, you play at different venues.“So, you have to prepare differently, think in a different way and that is the challenge,” he said.Kohli has confirmed that the 2027 ICC tournament will be his last World Cup for India. That decision has given his next campaign an added significance.“For me, it’s the last World Cup I’m going to play for India. And that is my motivation,” he added.
Article Summary: Virat Kohli recalls India's 2023 World Cup semifinal defeat to New Zealand. India lost by 18 runs after rain interrupted New Zealand's innings in the 47th over. Bhuvneshwar Kumar, who took three wickets in the game, recently described the defeat as "heartbreaking" Kohli has confirmed that the 2027 World Cup for India will be his last.

Article Title: Virat Kohli on the brink of history, 59 runs away from breaking Sachin Tendulkar's ODI record
Article Text:
Virat Kohli

Kohli set to rewrite fastest-to-15,000 record

West Indies have been one of Kohli's favourite opponents

Tendulkar's home record also within touching distance

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Virat Kohli is once again on the cusp of an ODI milestone that would add another remarkable chapter to his extraordinary career. The former India captain needs just 59 runs in the opening ODI against West Indies in Thiruvananthapuram on Sunday to become only the second batter in men's ODI history to reach the 15,000-run mark, joining Sachin Tendulkar in an exclusive club.Kohli has accumulated 14,941 runs in 314 ODIs and 302 innings at an average of 58.59, with 54 centuries and 79 fifties. Tendulkar remains the format's leading run-scorer with 18,426 runs, meaning Kohli's next landmark will place him alongside the player whose ODI records have defined Indian cricket for decades.But the 15,000-run mark is only one of several records within Kohli's reach.If Kohli scores the required 59 runs against West Indies, he will reach 15,000 ODI runs in his 303rd innings. That would make him the fastest batter to the landmark by a considerable margin. Tendulkar reached 15,000 runs in his 377th ODI innings in 2007. Kohli would therefore get there 74 innings earlier than his illustrious predecessor.The landmark would also fit into a pattern that has followed Kohli throughout his ODI career. He became the fastest batter to 13,000 ODI runs when he reached the mark in 267 innings in 2023, breaking Tendulkar's previous record of 321 innings.There is another layer to the milestone given the opposition. Kohli has enjoyed remarkable success against West Indies, scoring 2,261 runs in 43 matches and 41 innings at an average of 66.50. He has nine centuries and 11 fifties against them.Thiruvananthapuram has also been a productive venue for the right-hander. He has scored 199 runs without being dismissed in two ODIs at the venue, including his sensational unbeaten 166 against Sri Lanka in January 2023.Kohli has another Tendulkar record in his sights, the most ODI runs scored in home conditions. Tendulkar amassed 6,976 ODI runs in India. Kohli currently has 6,867, leaving him 110 runs short of overtaking the former India opener.Kohli's home ODI numbers underline his consistency. He has scored those 6,867 runs in 130 matches and 127 innings, averaging 62.42, with 27 centuries and 36 fifties.Kohli's pursuit of Tendulkar's records extends beyond ODIs. The former India captain currently has 85 international centuries and remains on the path towards the 100-century landmark that Tendulkar was the first to reach.At home, Kohli has 41 international hundreds, with Tendulkar's record standing at 42. Two more centuries in India would take Kohli past his former teammate and India's batting icon in that particular category.Kohli is also closing in on Tendulkar's record for most List-A centuries. Kohli has 59 List-A hundreds, while Tendulkar finished his career with 60. Since List-A cricket includes ODIs as well as other recognised 50-over matches, Kohli needs two more hundreds to move clear of Tendulkar at the top of the Indian list.
Article Summary: Virat Kohli needs 59 runs against West Indies in Thiruvananthapuram. Kohli has scored 14,941 runs in 314 ODIs and 302 innings at an average of 58.59. Tendulkar remains the format's leading run-scorer with 18,426 runs.

He faces competition from Alwar DCA president Mohit Yadav, son of BJP MLA Dr Jaswant Singh Yadav, who is double-filing for both vice-president and secretary.The secretarial contest also features Ashish Tiwari, son of Rajya Sabha MP Ghanshyam Tiwari, who has simultaneously staked a claim for the treasurer’s role. Article Title: Shubman Gill's captaincy of installments and path to 2027 World Cup
Article Text:
Shubman Gill (BCCI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

THIRUVANANTHAPURAM: Shubman Gill copped a blow to his right elbow at the nets on Friday, two days before India’s ODI opener against West Indies at the Greenfield International Stadium. Batting coach Sitanshu Kotak brushed off concerns, saying: “He is fine. ”It’s a scare India could do without, given how central Gill has become to this side. When he walks out for the toss on Sunday against his West Indies counterpart Shai Hope, it’ll look like a routine bilateral opener. It isn’t. The series puts the spotlight on India’s ODI captain, now leading a dressing room that includes Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli , the very players he once watched from the fringes.It’s a captaincy earned in installments. Gill holds two of India’s three leadership roles — Tests and ODIs — while Shreyas Iyer runs T20Is, a deliberate split-format call. Gill led India to a home sweep of Afghanistan in June — the Test 1-0, the ODIs 3-0 — and picked up Player of the Series for his own 238 runs. But results since have wobbled: India lost the ODI series in England in July 1-2, and a home series against New Zealand slipped 2-1 the visitors’ way earlier this year. This tour is a chance to settle those questions on home turf.With the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa now on the horizon, every game doubles as a trial.Ravindra Jadeja and Mohammed Siraj are fighting to reclaim spots. Uncapped players like Auqib Nabi and Naman Dhir are pushing for their first look-in. Gill's captaincy is being tested right alongside them.At 27, he's now the man deciding where two of the format's most decorated batters fit into the order. His approach has been simple — treat Rohit and Virat as senior pros with more to give, not legends to be managed around, and let his own bat do the talking.The numbers back him: 3,379 ODI runs at 60.33 from 67 games, nine centuries, and a 208 that made him the youngest double-centurion in ODI history. Against West Indies, his average climbs to 66.20, and his recent form — 84 and an unbeaten 154 against Afghanistan, then 80, 31 and 77 in England — suggests he’s in no mood to slow down.The split-captaincy call came down to scheduling more than philosophy: Since the T20 and ODI World Cups don’t fall in the same year, selectors chose not to stretch one leader across formats. South Africa, 2027, is where this gamble will get its verdict.
Article Summary: Shubman Gill copped a blow to his right elbow at the nets on Friday, two days before India’s ODI opener against West Indies at the Greenfield International Stadium. Batting coach Sitanshu Kotak brushed off concerns, saying: “He is fine. ”

Article Title: Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli: The Rolling Stones of Indian cricket still have one more song
Article Text:
Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli (BCCI Photo)

THIRUVANANTHAPURAM: Rohit Sharma turns 40 soon. Virat Kohli isn’t far behind — 38 in a couple of months. Most cricketers this age would have hung up their boots and slipped behind a commentary mic. Rohit and Virat haven’t. They continue to turn up at the nets, working just as hard and matching the efforts of teammates half their age.With their Tests and T20I careers well behind them, what remains now is the 50-over format, and they plan to keep playing ODIs with the 2027 World Cup as the final destination.The journey to next year’s showpiece tournament, jointly hosted by South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, passes through Thiruvananthapuram when India face the West Indies at the Greenfield International Stadium on Sunday.Kohli, the leading century-maker in ODIs with 54 tons, has asserted that next year’s World Cup would mark the end of his India career, and he is determined to pour everything he has into one final push for the title.“For me, it’s the last World Cup I’m going to play for India,” Kohli told JioStar. “The goal is absolutely to win the World Cup, and whatever it takes, I’m absolutely ready,” he said.Two months ago, Rohit shut down talks about retirement with a masterful 138 in the third ODI against England at Lord’s.Watching Rohit and Virat, you don’t get the sense of two cricketers slowing down, but of two musicians refusing to fade away.Just like Mick Jagger and Keith Richards. Jagger possessed the theatre and swagger. Richards was riff and rhythm. They are the iconic Rolling Stones. Virat is the Jagger, with his intensity. Rohit is calm and languid.For two decades, they shared dressing rooms and faced several ups and downs. Yet, it is the contrast that makes their partnership compelling.Like artists choosing their final canvas, Rohit and Virat have chosen ODIs, a format that is long enough to reward experience and demanding enough to test their fitness and stamina. By narrowing their focus to just one format, it makes every ODI between now and the 2027 World Cup a riveting watch. India are scheduled to play atleast 25 ODIs in this period.India’s bowling coach Morne Morkel admitted the team is “fortunate” to have their experience. “It’s always great to have that experience back in the team, to guide Shubman (Gill) as well.” Rohit and Virat would also exchange knowledge with greenhorns Naman Dhir and Aquib Nabi.“If Virat and Rohit are leading the conversation, there’s a lot of experience in those conversations that can be great for the team,” Morkel said about the synergy.On Sunday, Thiruvananthapuram will be more than just another stop on the calendar. Expect showstoppers Rohit and Virat to put on a show.
Article Summary: Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli will turn 40 soon. Most cricketers this age would have hung up their boots and slipped behind a commentary mic. They continue to turn up at the nets, working just as hard and matching the efforts of teammates half their age.

Article Title: ‘There is so much competition’: Kotak says it’s not ‘unfair’ to Jaiswal, tells him to ‘keep working hard and waiting’
Article Text:
Yashasvi Jaiswal (ANI Photo)

‘He should keep working hard and waiting’

Rohit, Kohli bringing ‘experience’ into World Cup build-up

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Jadeja ‘very much in the mix’

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think Yashasvi Jaiswal exclusion from the squad for the England tour was fair? Yes, it was fair No, it was not fair 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: India batting coach Sitanshu Kotak has backed Yashasvi Jaiswal to continue working hard and wait for his opportunities, insisting that the young opener’s limited chances in the ODI format should not be viewed as “unfair” treatment.Jaiswal played all three ODIs against Afghanistan at home but was left out of the squad for the subsequent tour of England. The left-hander has, however, returned to the 15-member squad for the three-match ODI series against the West Indies, which begins on Sunday.With Rohit Sharma and captain Shubman Gill likely to remain India’s first-choice opening combination, Jaiswal could once again have to wait for a regular run in the 50-over format.Kotak acknowledged the intense competition for places but made it clear that India continue to value Jaiswal.“I think there is so much competition (for team spots) and so many players are performing. Jaiswal…we all know he is one of the best batters and whenever he gets an opportunity he performs. So he is part of the team,” Kotak told reporters on the eve of the first ODI.The batting coach said the support staff were continuing to work with Jaiswal on his game while pointing out that even outstanding players can find themselves waiting when competition for places is fierce.“As a support staff, we look after his skills, practise and his mindset and Gautam (Gambhir) also talks to him a lot, but sometimes you see, say if (for example) there are three very good wicketkeepers, only one can play,” Kotak said.“So, it is not that somebody has been unfair to him. He should keep working hard and waiting for the opportunity and so far whenever he has been getting the opportunity, he has performed,” he added.Jaiswal’s presence in the squad also comes as India begin shaping their plans for the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa, with Rohit and Virat Kohli still targeting the global showpiece.Kotak believes the presence of senior players can be particularly valuable for youngsters such as Jaiswal as India gradually build towards the World Cup.“See, it is all about selling experience. They always do that. Whenever I have seen all the experienced players, even Gautam because he was playing, the level they have experienced, and when they see some player is going through a similar condition or situation, they always talk to them,” he said.“I think selling experience or selling whatever you have learnt is a great thing to do because it is getting knowledge or refreshing your knowledge as well.”Kotak said India’s planning would be conducted series by series, with the aim of exposing the squad to different conditions before the World Cup.“So from now on, our plan is to do (planning) series by series. Luckily, we have a New Zealand series where it is outside Asia. So, there will be some different conditions - moisture, grass, all will be different,” he said.“If we can successfully do that, within a year's time we should be ready for any challenges, any different wickets or any different bowling attacks,” he added.Ravindra Jadeja ’s return to the white-ball squad after an eight-month gap has also added experience to India’s World Cup planning. Kotak said the veteran all-rounder remains firmly in contention.“Jadeja is an outstanding bowler. We all know his records... Jadeja is one of the best fielders on a world level. The experience he has…I actually firmly believe that experience is something you cannot beat,” he said.“Like we see Rohit and Virat, we see Jadeja, they bring a lot to the team,” Kotak added.Kotak also confirmed that Gill is fit for Sunday’s opener after being hit on his right elbow by Mohammed Siraj during training.“Gill is looking good, I think he is good to go tomorrow,” he said.
Article Summary: Jaiswal played all three ODIs against Afghanistan but was left out of the squad for the subsequent tour of England. The left-hander has, however, returned to the 15-member squad. India begin shaping their plans for the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa.

Article Title: ‘It’s the last World Cup I’m going to play for India’: Virat Kohli vows to give everything
Article Text:

One last World Cup, one clear goal

NEW DELHI: Virat Kohli has revealed that the 2027 ODI World Cup will be his last World Cup for India, with the prospect of one final shot at the coveted trophy providing the biggest motivation for the batting stalwart.Kohli, who now plays only ODI cricket at the international level, said he is ready to leave everything on the field as India begin their preparations for the 50-over showpiece in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.Speaking to JioStar ahead of India's ODI series against West Indies, Kohli underlined the unique physical and mental demands of a 50-over World Cup and made it clear that winning the title is his ultimate objective.“The intensity of a 50-over World Cup is greater than anything. Because now, it's about 10 games at a T20 level of intensity. But you are playing 2.5 T20 games in one day. And to maintain that intensity for 10 games in a big tournament and World Cup is a big deal,” Kohli said.“Also now, it's in foreign conditions. It takes a lot out of you. For me, it's the last World Cup I'm going to play for India. And that is my motivation. Like, you know, to leave everything out there.And of course, the goal is absolutely to win the World Cup. And whatever it takes, I'm absolutely ready.”The 2027 World Cup will give Kohli another opportunity to chase the trophy in what he has now confirmed will be his final ODI World Cup campaign for India.Kohli was part of India's triumphant 2011 World Cup campaign and also played in the 2023 final, where India lost to Australia in Ahmedabad. Across his World Cup career, he has scored 1,795 runs in 37 matches at an average of 59.83, including five centuries and 12 fifties.His overall ODI record stands at 14,941 runs in 302 innings at an average of 58.59, with 54 centuries and 79 fifties.But individual numbers are clearly secondary to Kohli as he looks towards his final World Cup.The 2027 World Cup will be jointly hosted by South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia from October 4 to November 21.India's ODI preparations begin with the three-match home series against West Indies, followed by further 50-over assignments as the team builds towards the global tournament.
Article Summary: Virat Kohli confirms 2027 ODI World Cup will be his last campaign for India. Kohli says he is ready to leave everything on the field as India begin preparations for 50-over showpiece in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia. India's ODI preparations begin with three-match home series against West Indies.

Article Title: Mayank Yadav: Rebuilding the 150kph dream, with an eye on the 2027 ODI World Cup
Article Text:
Mayank Yadav bowls against Zimbabwe. (AP)

NEW DELHI:

മായങ്ക് യാദവ്

With Mayank, the first thing was how we can gradually increase his workload. And once his workload hits the peak, how do we manage it at that level so that it does not come down? Gaurav Sharma | Head Physio, Gujarat Titans

मयंक यादव दिल्ली प्रीमियर लीग

मयंक यादव

Poll Vote & Share your view Should Mayank be included in the 2027 ODI World Cup squad? Yes, if he stays fit No, he needs more time 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A video of Mayank Yadav training with Team India’s Test and ODI captain Shubman Gill in Mohali went viral recently on social media. It comes on the heels of the tearaway quick shifting his training base to Chandigarh, where he is working with Gaurav Sharma , the city-based physio who also serves as the head physio of IPL franchise Gujarat Titans (GT).“He reached out to me after IPL 2026. Before going to Zimbabwe, he trained in Chandigarh for three weeks. He got the desired results, and he is (now) training for the upcoming West Indies series,” Sharma tells TimesofIndia.com.Mayank has had a terrible couple of years since bursting onto the scene during IPL 2024, where he impressed with his raw pace. Then a spate of injuries derailed his career. Last year, during one of the Ranji Trophy matches at the Arun Jaitley Stadium, he joked: “Lumbar stress fracture, lower back spasm, toe injury, side strain, hamstring... rehne do bhaiya, list lambi (the list is long),” he told this reporter while getting into his car outside the stadium.Mayank’s injury woes have been compounded by freak setbacks, with the fast bowler twice picking up a new injury while recovering from another. In May 2025, for instance, he injured his toe after accidentally jamming it against the side of his bed, resulting in a laceration that later became infected.He made his comeback during IPL 2026, where his pace was low, and the trolling was immediate. Former West Indies pacer Ian Bishop came to Mayank’s defence.“To see negative comments about Mayank Yadav today is horrifying. The kid nearly lost his career & livelihood at 21yrs. Just to see him play again is huge boost. The fact that he clocked 150kph again is a miracle. At 23yrs just pray for him that he stays fit. The control will come,” Bishop wrote on X.Now, a few months later, those tracking his development closely say the youngster is consistently touching the 150kph mark again.“At this moment, Mayank is doing really well. He had a back injury. He underwent surgery for the same, and the body takes time. At present, he has no injury. I am just taking care of him so that he does not pick up any injury going forward,” says Sharma, who has also worked with Arshdeep Singh, Gurnoor Brar, Naman Dhir and Prabhsimran Singh, to name a few.“The second thing is that we are working on his workload management. We are increasing the load slowly and steadily, and he is working on it very well,” says Sharma.Mayank last played in the Delhi Premier League (DPL), where he featured in seven matches for East Delhi Riders and picked up eight wickets.It has been learnt that Mayank is bowling 10 overs in three and a half hours during his training. The spells are divided into three. With the new ball, Mayank is bowling five overs, then three, and finishes it up with two overs. Out of the 60 balls he bowls daily, he consistently touches the 150kph mark, while his average speed remains in the higher 140s.Devender Sharma, who has worked with Mayank during his formative years, says Mayank has been told to be ready for the 2027 ODI World Cup.“They want him to be ready for longer formats as well. He is bowling close to 12-15 overs per day for the last six months or so,” says Devender.Gaurav explains how he has planned out a programme for Mayank and how he is going through it day by day.“With Mayank, the first thing was how we can gradually increase his workload. And once his workload hits the peak, how do we manage it at that level so that it does not come down?” he explains.“So, this is a day-by-day process. We assess what we want to see, and then we are able to do what we want them to do. That allows us to progress day by day.”Above all, Sharma feels it is all about confidence, especially when it comes to Mayank, who has gone through so many injuries in his young career.“Definitely, working with a fast bowler is a challenge. With a fast bowler, there are very different biomechanics, so the chances of injury are higher. If we take into account the toll on the joints, muscles and body, and understand the mechanics of the bowler, his action and his lifestyle, then it becomes easier to work with him,” he says.“And when it comes to Mayank, we are talking about an India player. The most important thing for them is confidence. He wants to know whether I am able to give him that confidence and whether I have the answer to the question he has come to me with. I have to be very truthful with myself.“If I am giving an answer, I have to be absolutely sure that the answer is right. It cannot be hypothetical. If I am research-oriented and I know what I am doing, I should also be able to prove it in the future. That is the most important thing. Then, day by day, when we work together, that trust is built because the results of the assessment become visible. That is how things work,” he adds.For Mayank, the road back is no longer about proving how fast he can bowl. He has already shown that he can set the speed guns on fire. The bigger challenge now is sustaining that pace, building the workload required for the longer formats and, most importantly, staying on the park. With the 2027 ODI World Cup in the near future, the process has begun.

Injury woes have been compounded by freak setbacks, with the fast bowler twice picking up a new injury while recovering from another. Former West Indies pacer Ian Bishop came to Mayank’s defence.

Article Title: Asian Games: PV Sindhu, Unnati Hooda exits cap disappointing badminton campaign as India return with just one medal
Article Text:
PV Sindhu and Unnati Hooda

Sindhu fades after strong start against Chen

Hooda fights back but Yamaguchi holds on

Doubles pairs also fall in quarterfinals

Heavy schedule adds to players’ workload

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India’s badminton campaign at the Asian Games 2026 ended on Sunday with a disappointing return of just one medal, as PV Sindhu and Unnati Hooda bowed out in the women’s singles quarterfinals after spirited efforts against formidable opponents.Two-time Olympic medallist Sindhu went down 21-11, 18-21, 10-21 to Tokyo Olympic champion Chen Yu Fei of China, while 19-year-old Hooda pushed three-time world champion Akane Yamaguchi of Japan before losing 16-21, 21-14, 17-21.The exits meant India failed to win a medal in any of the individual badminton events, with the men’s team bronze remaining the country’s only podium finish at Aichi-Nagoya. The contrast with the previous edition in Hangzhou was stark: India had won three medals there, including men’s team silver, Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty’s doubles gold, and HS Prannoy’s singles bronze.Sindhu, who had already played twice on Saturday, was competing for the third time in less than 24 hours. She started strongly against Chen, taking control of the opening game with sharp movement and aggressive shot-making to win it 21-11.The Indian also stayed in contention through much of the second game, which was closely fought and featured long rallies. The pair were level at 16-16 before Chen edged ahead to take the game 21-18 and force a decider.Chen seized control in the third, opening up an early lead and taking an 11-7 advantage at the interval. Sindhu managed only three more points after the break as the Chinese won 10 of the next 11 points to close out the match.Sindhu had entered the quarterfinal with a 7-9 head-to-head record against Chen, whom she had beaten on the way to winning the Japan Open Super 750 title in July. But the Indian could not repeat that result after a demanding schedule over the previous day.Hooda also showed resilience in her quarterfinal against world No. 3 Yamaguchi, recovering from a one-sided opening game to take the second and force a decider.The Japanese controlled the early exchanges in the first game, using a range of strokes to build a sizeable lead and eventually take it 21-16. Hooda responded with a strong attacking display in the second, pulling level at 7-7 and then moving ahead as Yamaguchi began making errors. The Indian won eight successive points to claim the game 21-14.The decider remained tight, with the players level at 5-5 before Yamaguchi established a lead. Hooda continued to extend rallies and challenge the Japanese, but Yamaguchi held her advantage and closed out the match 21-17.India’s remaining doubles hopes had ended earlier on Sunday. Women’s pair Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand, fresh from winning a maiden World Championships bronze last month, lost 18-21, 9-21 to Malaysia’s world No. 5 combination of Pearly Tan and Thinaah Muralitharan.In mixed doubles, Dhruv Kapila and Tanisha Crasto came close to upsetting the world No. 1 Chinese pair of Feng Yan Zhe and Huang Dongping, but eventually lost 14-21, 21-18, 18-21.The demanding schedule was another talking point, with Sindhu, Hooda and Ayush Shetty among the players required to contest two matches within a few hours on Saturday. Sindhu’s quarterfinal against Chen was her third match in less than 24 hours, while Hooda also faced a taxing turnaround before her last-eight clash.Despite the effort and resilience shown by India’s leading shuttlers, the campaign ended well short of the three-medal return from Hangzhou. With only the men’s team bronze to show from Aichi-Nagoya, India’s badminton contingent leaves the Games without an individual-event medal.
Article Summary: India's badminton campaign at the Asian Games 2026 ends with a disappointing return of just one medal. PV Sindhu and Unnati Hooda bowed out in the women's singles quarterfinals after spirited efforts against formidable opponents. India failed to win a medal in any of the individualBadminton events at Aichi-Nagoya.

Article Title: One point short in 2018, Trap Shooter Ahvar Rizvi gets his Asian Games chance eight years later
Article Text:
Ahvar Rizvi

From a Double Trap gun to a borrowed Trap gun

The borrowed gun that took him to the Asian Games

Away from the range, he is in the fields

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

In 2018, Ahvar Rizvi missed India's Asian Games selection by one point. He was competing in Double Trap then, an event in which he had established himself as one of India's promising young shooters. At the World Championships in Changwon that year, Rizvi won the junior Double Trap title. The Asian Games place, though, went elsewhere."I missed the Asian Games by one point," Rizvi told TOI Sports. "I was very sad because there is a competition once every four years, and it is a big competition. You miss that, so then I didn't understand what to do."There was another problem. Double Trap was subsequently removed from the international programme, leaving Rizvi to move to Trap in 2019."I struggled a lot when Double Trap was closed," he said. "I had been in the team continuously for six or seven years, and then suddenly I was out of the team."Seven years later, Rizvi is back in an Indian team for the Asian Games. This time, in Trap. The 26-year-old from Mahalgaon, Meerut, is preparing for his first appearance at the continental Games after making India's 2026 men's Trap squad alongside Kynan Chenai and Shapath Bharadwaj - the bronze medallist at the Juniors, in which Rizvi had claimed gold in 2018."It took me seven or eight years to get here," Rizvi said. "So this is my first international trap event and my first Asian Games. So I am feeling very proud. I am going to play for India. I will keep India's flag high there."Rizvi had started shooting because shooting was already part of the family. His father, uncles and cousins shot. As a child, he used air guns before asking his father if he could take up shotgun shooting. His father initially felt he was too young for the recoil of a 12-bore."There was a lot of recoil in the 12-bore. I was small and very thin at that time, so my father told me not to do it yet," Rizvi said.He went to his uncle instead. "When I came here, I qualified at the state level. When I reached home, all the family members were standing there with flowers for me. They welcomed me."He then qualified for the pre-nationals and nationals. He still did not have his own gun. His cousin Raiyan Rizvi let him use his. "I didn't have a gun, so my cousin Raiyan, whom I just told you about, used to let me use his," he said.Rizvi was too young to have a licence. The gun was also physically large for him. "When I was competing in the nationals, the gun was bigger than me," he said. "My cousin used to stand behind me. When the recoil came, he would push me back. So he used to stand behind me to support me."That was the beginning. The Indian team came next, followed by the junior world title in Double Trap in 2018. Then the event disappeared and Rizvi had to learn Trap."I kept doing it, but my coach, Vikram [Singh Chopra] sir , who was always with me and supported me, never told me that I had shifted from double trap and that I couldn't do it," he said. "He always told me that I would be able to do it."It took years before Rizvi felt he understood the new event. "After two or three years, I started to understand what trap was."The scores still did not immediately follow. He missed selection by a few points in 2024 and again in 2025. There was also a point when he stopped shooting."There was a point in between when I quit because it was not happening," Rizvi said. "But when I represented India, I thought I would do it in the future."The equipment was another part of the rebuild. Rizvi's old Double Trap gun could not simply be carried over to Trap. He eventually got a Trap gun from teammate Lakshya Sheoran, the Asian Games silver medallist, and used it in nationals and trials for a year."Although I have a trap gun, this gun is not mine. This is my friend Lakshya’s gun. He is an Asian Games silver medallist," Rizvi said."So he has given me this gun. I have been competing in nationals and trials with his gun for a year." Rizvi now has his own stock, made in Italy and adjusted for competition."The stock is mine, and I have adjusted it for competition," he said. "I am seeing a lot of improvement since I changed my stock." The equipment was still being fine-tuned when he was preparing for the Asian Games."Vikram Sir, when we were in Italy for the World Cup, and I got my stock set up," Rizvi said. "I was a little worried about my equipment, but now I just have to focus 100 per cent on what I have to do."His 2026 international results show the work is still in progress. He finished 39th in Trap qualification at the Almaty World Cup with 115 and 47th at Lonato with 118. At Almaty, Rizvi and Pragati Dubey finished 23rd in the mixed team event with 130. The selection trials, though, gave him the opening he had been waiting for.And this time, there was no one-point calculation to make."I never thought that if I had got that one point at that time, it would have been different," Rizvi said of 2018. "It was just that I didn't get it then, so I was a little sad. Then I put it behind me and started again."His life away from shooting is rather different from what the range might suggest. Rizvi's family has been involved in shooting for years, but farming remains part of his everyday life."Ahvar Rizvi is a normal person. He is a son of a farmer, and if there is no shooting, he is in the fields with his father and elder brother," he said.The Asian Games, though, have been the thing he has been waiting for."We are in this game, and everyone's expectation when we go to an event is to bring gold," he said. "Gold will not come just because we are in the team. We have to work hard."There will be nervousness. Rizvi expects that. "There is excitement and nervousness when we play a match. But the main thing is to control it."His way of controlling it is to talk to his coach. "When I talk to my coach whenever I get nervous, I get a lot of relief and I stay focused."His first Asian Games comes after the competition he missed in 2018, the event he lost in Double Trap, the years spent trying to make sense of Trap and a selection process that finally went his way. He does not spend much time looking back."I went back and never looked back," he said. "Now it is 2028, and the Olympics are coming. Now I have my eyes on it."For Nagoya, though, his instructions are simpler."We get thoughts before shooting. We think when we are competing. Those thoughts come, but stopping them is very important.""If the target is going to be left, let it come. But we have to break. We have to hit the target.""Never give up. So this is my thought."
Article Summary: Ahvar Rizvi is back in an Indian team for the Asian Games. This time, in Trap. The 26-year-old from Mahalgaon, Meerut, is preparing for his first appearance at the continental Games after making India's 2026 men's Trap squad.
